message.content:
A CPU (Central Processing Unit) and a GPU (Graphics Processing Unit) are both processors, but they’re designed for different kinds of workloads:

| Feature | CPU | GPU |
|---------|-----|-----|
| **Purpose** | General‑purpose computing – handles everything from OS tasks to application logic. | Specialized for highly parallel tasks – originally for rendering graphics, now also used for scientific computing, machine learning, etc. |
| **Architecture** | Few cores (typically 2–32) with powerful out‑of‑order execution, large caches, complex control logic. | Hundreds or thousands of simpler cores optimized for SIMD (Single Instruction, Multiple Data). |
| **Instruction Set** | Complex instruction set (CISC) with many features (branch prediction, speculative execution). | Usually a reduced instruction set (RISC) focused on arithmetic and data movement. |
| **Memory Hierarchy** | Large L1/L2/L3 caches per core, sophisticated memory controllers. | Smaller per‑core caches; relies on high‑bandwidth memory (HBM, GDDR). |
| **Parallelism** | Thread‑level parallelism – a few threads run concurrently. | Data‑level parallelism – thousands of lightweight threads execute the same operation on different data. |
| **Typical Workloads** | Sequential tasks, branching logic, I/O, OS services. | Matrix/vector operations, image/video processing, deep‑learning inference/training, simulations. |
| **Performance Metrics** | FLOPS per core lower, but latency matters more. | FLOPS per core higher, throughput dominates. |
| **Energy Efficiency** | Optimized for low power per core, but overall power scales with number of cores. | Very efficient at high throughput; power consumption rises with core count but each core is cheap. |

In short, CPUs excel at tasks that require complex decision making and low latency, while GPUs shine when you need to perform the same operation on many data elements simultaneously. That’s why modern systems often combine both: the CPU handles general control flow, and the GPU accelerates compute‑heavy kernels.
